_comment: Web slide deck of the talk (/attribution/slides/), in talk order (talk/draft.md). Each content slide is read without the speaker: a title that states the claim, three to five bullets, optionally one formula, one number and one page figure, a takeaway line and a source line (page section, paper and locator); then the speaker's notes (cue lines of the draft) and the page anchor. Checked at build by src/scripts/slides.js.

slides.title: Explaining a trading P&L
slides.subtitle: What finance knows about performance attribution, and what is open
slides.author: Emmanuel Sérié
notes: Paste the link in the Teams chat.

slides.title: Attribution assigns the desk's P&L to signals, positions and costs
bullets: A P&L is an amount accumulated over an interval, positive or negative
Classification rates do not add up to a P&L in currency
Overlapping indicators count one episode twice unless a rule shares it
Whether to drop or resize a signal is a separate question
slides.takeaway: Contributions must sum to the P&L, with a residual for the rest
notes: Today's question: how much of the P&L goes to each signal, each position, each cost.
Three obstacles: a P&L accumulates over an interval, amounts must add up, indicators overlap.
Sections 1 to 3 share money. Section 4 shares what correlated indicators predict.
Every number comes from a published paper or our own simulation. No desk data.
“To follow the money, the desk first has to say which amount it wants to explain.”

slides.title: Four choices define the attribution before any split
bullets: Reference: a paper portfolio, or positions marked at the midprice
The reference sets the amount to explain, so contributions change with it
Interval, information and indicator kind fix the remaining terms of the split
The residual is reported as its own term
slides.takeaway: A sum that closes checks the accounting; it explains nothing alone
notes: Four choices before any split: reference, interval, information, indicator kind.
The reference sets what we subtract, so it changes the amount to explain.
The residual gets its own bar. A sum that closes checks the accounting, not a cause.
For this desk: one set of fill records for physical and financial positions, by delivery quarter-hour.

slides.title: An attribution depends on what was known at each decision
bullets: Ex ante: exposures and a risk model recorded before returns occur
Ex post: the same exposures combined with realised returns
Grinold and Kahn judge skill on bets declared in advance
Exposures fitted after the P&L test an explanation chosen with hindsight
Currency P&L adds up across periods; percentage returns compound
slides.takeaway: Working in currency avoids linking rules, yet still needs reference prices
notes: Timing: a forecast known at decision time is an input. Tomorrow's forecast error is an outcome.

slides.title: Signals drive trades; state indicators describe market conditions
bullets: A signal enters the policy and may change its trades
Spread, volatility and market order flow are state indicators
Inventory and own orders come from the signals, so they belong with the policy
A volatility forecast fed to the policy is a signal; realised volatility, a state indicator
slides.takeaway: Section 2.5 splits the fill records; section 4 relates each part to state indicators
notes: A signal enters the algorithm and changes trades. A state indicator only describes the market.

slides.title: Brinson splits active return into allocation, selection and interaction
bullets: Portfolio 60% in segment A, 40% in B; the benchmark holds the reverse
Segment returns: benchmark 600 and 200 bp, portfolio 800 and 100 bp
Allocation weights segments differently; selection picks better stocks within them
Folding interaction into selection changes the terms, never the total

number.label: allocation, selection and interaction sum to the active return

slides.takeaway: The total is fixed; the split depends on the convention
notes: Brinson: allocation 80, selection 20, interaction 60. Together they make the 160 basis points.

slides.title: Euler's theorem splits portfolio volatility into contributions that add up
bullets: Returns split additively; risk does not, because positions co-move
Volatility scales with the portfolio, so Euler's theorem applies
Each contribution depends on the position's covariance with the whole portfolio
Litterman's hot-spots report lists them next to the position sizes
A hedge can contribute negatively; the largest position need not dominate
slides.takeaway: The split allocates volatility, not the realised P&L of a day
notes: Euler: the risk contributions add up to the volatility. A hedge can be negative.
“Your forecasting models already produce attributions, so here is what those attributions measure.”

slides.title: For correlated indicators, the game sets what a share means
bullets: The policy may ignore state indicators, or we may be unable to rerun it
A fitted model then links the indicators to an outcome, such as daily P&L
A game gives the value $v(S)$ of every subset $S$ of indicators
Shapley share: an indicator's gain on joining, averaged over all orders of entry
slides.takeaway: The game sets the units, baseline and meaning of each share
notes: Your libraries give SHAP values. Here the algorithm may not read the indicators, so no reruns.
The diagram uses the conditional game. Most libraries compute the interventional one.

slides.title: Coefficients swing between near-copies; Shapley gives each about half
bullets: A regression predicts the joint effect of near-copies well, yet cannot separate them
At high correlation, A's coefficient runs from about −0.9 to 2.5
Their sum stays near 2: the data fix only what the pair does together
Shapley of $R^2$ refits each subset's regression and averages over orders

number.label: A's Shapley share of what the pair explains

slides.takeaway: A stable share is neither causal nor a test of significance
slides.source: §4.1; Lipovetsky and Conklin (2001, Table II, p. 329)
notes: As the two indicators become alike, the coefficients swing and their sum stays near 2.
Shapley on R squared gives A about half. Stable, but neither causal nor significant.

slides.title: A SHAP value splits a forecast; a P&L share splits money
bullets: Refitted $R^2$: shares of the day-to-day variation a regression fits
Local SHAP: one day's prediction minus the average, in the model's units
Interventional SHAP explains the model; conditional SHAP also credits correlated indicators
SAGE: the reduction in prediction error when the model uses these indicators
slides.takeaway: These shares measure predictive information, not realised P&L
notes: A SHAP value splits a forecast in its own units. A share of P&L splits money.

slides.title: A top share counts only if it beats the top share on shuffled P&L
bullets: A model fitted to noise still returns shares, and one of them is largest
Block shuffling keeps the P&L's time dependence and breaks its link to indicators
Comparing top share with top share accounts for picking the largest
Knockoffs give each indicator a fair competitor; they select variables, allocating no profit
slides.takeaway: The comparison says whether any indicator predicts the outcome
notes: Null comparison: shuffle the P&L in blocks and recompute. The top share must beat that.
“To split money, we go back to the book itself.”

slides.title: Signal attribution needs reruns of the policy or its equations
bullets: The portfolio holds one position built from $K$ forecasts, the signals
One signal's purchase may reinforce another, offset it, or change nothing
Stand-alone proxies, leave-one-out and Shapley need a policy we can rerun
Durin and Grinold–Easton need a known optimiser and its multipliers
slides.takeaway: A signal's contribution means something different in each method, because the inputs differ
notes: The fill records, the ledger of section 2.5, split by leg or fill. No optimiser.

slides.title: Durin splits the optimiser's position into one position per signal
bullets: With the binding constraints fixed, the optimal trade is affine in the forecasts
Each signal's trade responds to its forecast and the position it already holds
The signal positions add up to the joint position, with no rerun
Each signal receives its piece's P&L and a share of joint risk and cost
slides.takeaway: It needs a known convex optimiser with a quadratic risk or cost term
notes: By signal: the optimiser's equations, as in Durin, or reruns of the policy.

slides.title: In a linear book, holdings and signal splits sum to the same P&L
bullets: Assumed: mean-variance book, no trading cost, no position bound
$\gamma$ and $\Sigma$ frozen at their realised values, so no rerun
$X$, by holdings: asset $i$ receives $x_i r_i$ of the gross P&L
$D$, by signals: signal $k$ receives $\gamma^{-1}(g^k)^\top\Sigma^{-1}r$
One forecast per asset, coalitions keep the full $\Sigma^{-1}$: Shapley gives $(X_i+D_i)/2$
slides.formula: x=\gamma^{-1}\Sigma^{-1}G,\quad G=\sum_k g^k,\quad \sum_i X_i=\sum_k D_k=x^\top r
slides.takeaway: A game removing only signals gives $D$; start/stop constraints fall outside
notes: Linear book: split by holdings X, split by signals D. Both sum to the P&L, no rerun.

slides.title: Shapley averages each signal's gain over every order of entry
bullets: A coalition's value is the P&L of a rerun with only its signals
Stand-alone value: the signal's marginal contribution when it enters first
Leave-one-out: its marginal contribution when it enters last
The shares sum to the full P&L minus the reference policy's P&L

number.label: coalition values for eight signals, by exact enumeration

slides.takeaway: Up to eight signals, no sampler needed fewer values than exact enumeration
notes: Shapley averages over every order. Stand-alone is the signal first, leave-one-out the signal last.
The cost is two to the K backtests. Up to eight signals, enumerate exactly.

slides.title: With a large spread, stand-alone proxies miss what signals earn together
bullets: Durin rejects proxy regressions as a general method: binding constraints leave residuals
At a spread of 2.0 std(G), three of four signals never trade alone
Together they clear the spread; Durin's split pays all four signals
Base case: proxy distance from Durin 0.19, Shapley games 0.045 and 0.037

number.label: of P&L variance in the proxy residual, base case

slides.takeaway: Joint trades that no proxy mix matches end in the residual
notes: §3.5: the P&L paths figure on the large-spread scenario, then the bar figure across seeds.
Large spread: three of four signals never trade alone. The proxy sees nothing, together they earn.

slides.title: Across seeds, both Shapley games stay within 0.12 of Durin
bullets: Durin is the benchmark here, because its split is exact for this optimiser
Larger spread, more signals or higher correlation push proxy shares away
The proxy residual grows along the same sweeps
Whiskers show dispersion across seeds, not the uncertainty for a real desk

number.label: half-L1 distance between Shapley and Durin mean shares

slides.takeaway: Agreement with Durin does not make a contribution the only correct one
notes: “That leaves two research projects, one on the amounts and one on the signals.”

slides.title: Two research projects start in simulation, where the answer is known
bullets: 5.1 Fill records: the markout horizon that sets the reference price
5.2 Signals: when a cheap method can replace full reruns
5.3 Later: state indicators and policies without usable equations
Projects 5.1 and 5.2 fix in advance the result that would stop them
slides.takeaway: A planted answer lets each method be checked against the truth
notes: One row per project: question, decision, first experiment, stop rule.
Both start in simulation, where the answer is known.

slides.title: The reference price moves money between spread and positioning
bullets: One purchase at €99.98; midprice €100.00 before the fill, €99.95 after
Fee €0.01; P&L after fees, marked at the later midprice, is −€0.04
Reference before the fill: net spread +€0.01, positioning −€0.05
Reference at the later midprice: net spread −€0.04, positioning zero

number.label: marked P&L after fees, under either reference

slides.takeaway: Menkveld's market maker: €1.55 per trade net spread, −€0.68 positioning
notes: One fill: mid 100, we buy at 99.98 with a one-cent fee, then mid 99.95.
Minus four cents: plus one net spread, minus five positioning; against the later mid, minus four net spread, zero positioning.

slides.title: The markout horizon where reversion stops sets the reference price
bullets: Desks measure markouts at 1 s, 10 s, 1 min, 5 min and longer
The simulation plants a permanent price impact and a transitory one
The price move up to that horizon should recover the planted impact
We stop if the miss exceeds a tolerance fixed in advance, say ±10%
slides.takeaway: Without that check, the split adds up yet hides losses to informed counterparties
notes: Markouts from one second to five minutes show when the price move after a fill stops reverting.
The markout horizon sets the reference. We plant a known permanent impact and stop if we miss it.
“Once the amounts are fixed, the second project asks how much each signal earned.”

slides.title: Three uses of a signal attribution need three different quantities
bullets: Reporting: Shapley shares over reruns, above a declared reference policy
Dropping: net P&L lost when only that signal is removed, on held-out days
Resizing: the value of a small change in the signal's weight
Target: all three computed from every rerun on the simulator
One-history 90% error bars must contain the many-history average in 90% of histories
slides.takeaway: We stop if no cheap method meets its tolerance near the desk's settings
notes: Three uses, three numbers: Shapley to report, removal loss to drop, a marginal value to resize.
On a simulator all three are exact. We measure how far each cheap method sits.
Error bars from one history must contain the many-history average nine times in ten.
We stop if no cheap method meets its tolerance, or if the bars do not cover.

slides.title: Later work: state indicators and policies without usable equations
bullets: State indicators: relate spread and inventory P&L to market conditions
These shares divide predictive information, not realised P&L
Opaque policies: a surrogate must first reproduce the policy on held-out cases
Each removal operator on the surrogate's inputs defines a different attribution
slides.takeaway: Their stopping rules will be set once 5.1 and 5.2 have results
notes: Later: spread and inventory P&L against market conditions, and policies whose rules we cannot read.
“That brings us to what the desk could test first.”

slides.title: The citation graph places each paper read by year and topic
bullets: Papers sit by year, left to right, in three topic bands
Bands: classical attribution and risk; signals and Shapley; market making and execution
Filled circles are papers this page cites
Arrows point from a paper to the papers it cites
Twelve other cited works are not drawn
slides.takeaway: Selecting a paper shows its summary and the sections that cite it
notes: The graph: year left to right, one band per theme, filled circles are the papers cited.

slides.title: The page links its code, data and references
notes: An attribution starts with reference, interval, information and indicators.
SHAP splits a forecast, a P&L share splits money. By signal needs equations or reruns.
First step: split the fill records (section 2.5, project 5.1); it needs no optimiser.
The QR code opens the page, with the code or data behind every figure.
“To open the discussion: how does the desk define its P&L, and which records does it already keep?”
